title: Docker for a Node service

story: The gateway, our only door to Claude, holds the Anthropic key, and every agent's model call passes through it. It runs as a container on our internal cluster. Its first Dockerfile was four lines: FROM node:24, copy everything, npm install, start. It worked. It also ran as root, carried a compiler, the whole source and every test tool, and could write anywhere on its own disk.

Think about what that means on a bad day. A bug in one dependency lets an attacker run a single command inside the container. As root, with a writable disk and a full toolbox, that one command can download more tools, change the gateway's code on disk so it copies the key somewhere, and stay there. And on a quieter day, the node:24 tag pointed at a new image over a weekend, and Monday's build behaved differently although nobody had changed a line.
hook.question: How do I build an image for a service that holds keys, so that the same build always gives the same image, and a process that is taken over inside it can do almost nothing?

read.h: Build in one stage, run in another
p: An image is a frozen filesystem plus the command to start; a container is a running copy of it. A Dockerfile builds the image step by step, and each step becomes a layer that Docker reuses when its inputs did not change. That is why we copy package.json and the lockfile first and run npm ci, and only then copy the source: editing a .ts file then skips the slow install.

Building needs things that running does not: TypeScript, the type definitions, the source. So the Dockerfile has two stages. The first stage, named build, installs everything, runs tsc and then removes the dev dependencies with npm prune. The second stage starts again from a clean base and copies in only what runs: package.json, the production node_modules and dist/. No compiler, no source, no tests. Every tool that is not in the final image is a tool an attacker cannot use.

code.text:
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:a5f4366e… AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json .npmrc ./
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src src
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev --ignore-scripts

FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:a5f4366e…
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist dist
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

notes.text: Node 24 on Debian bookworm, slim variant, pinned by digest (next section). This stage is named build.
Only the files npm ci needs. They change rarely, so this layer is usually reused.
Exactly the lockfile, and no install scripts from packages (lesson p1-1).
tsc writes dist/, then the dev dependencies are removed.
The second stage starts clean. Nothing from the first stage comes along unless it is copied.
Copy from the build stage, not from your laptop.
From here on, and for the running process, the user is 10001 instead of root.
The exec form: node runs directly as the container's main process, with no shell in between.

read.h: Pin the base image by digest
p: A tag such as node:24-bookworm-slim is a name that moves: when a new Node patch or Debian fix comes out, the tag points at a new image. That is how Monday's build changed without a change in our repo. A digest is a hash of the image's content, written sha256:…, so it can only ever mean those exact bytes.

docker pull prints the digest, and the FROM line carries it after an @. Now the base only changes when a pull request changes the digest, and a reviewer sees it, which is the same rule as exact versions in package.json. Updating the digest is routine work that a bot such as Renovate can open pull requests for.

code.text:
docker pull node:24-bookworm-slim
DIGEST=$(docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' node:24-bookworm-slim | cut -d@ -f2)
echo $DIGEST

notes.text: Fetches the image the tag points at today and prints its digest.
Reads the digest again from the local image, without a network call, and keeps only the part after the @.

read.see:
Digest: sha256:a5f4366e834695d5f363b920c104953a535d3a9864d1bdf74566a0ebe01daee5
Status: Image is up to date for node:24-bookworm-slim
(yours may be newer, and that is fine: pin the one you see)

read.h: Run it locked, then prove the locks
p: USER 10001 in the Dockerfile means the process is not root: it is a user with no name and no rights, and the files in /app belong to root, so it cannot change its own code. Three flags on docker run close the rest. --read-only makes the container's whole filesystem read-only, so nothing can be written anywhere. --cap-drop ALL removes Linux capabilities, the small pieces of root power that a process can hold even without being root. --security-opt no-new-privileges stops any program inside from gaining more rights than it started with.

Do not trust the flags; test them. docker exec runs a command inside the running container, so you can ask who the process is and try to write a file. If a service really needs scratch space, give it a small in-memory folder with --tmpfs /tmp, and everything else stays read-only. On the cluster, where Kubernetes runs each container inside a pod, the same locks are written into the pod's securityContext as runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and dropped capabilities, so they hold even when nobody types docker run.

code.text:
docker run -d --name svc -p 8080:8080 --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges svc:dev
docker exec svc id
docker exec svc touch /app/x

notes.text: Read-only filesystem, no capabilities, no way to gain privileges.
Who is the process? It should not be uid 0, which is root.
Try to change the app's own folder.

read.see:
uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001
touch: cannot touch '/app/x': Read-only file system

p: Docker and Kubernetes stop a container the same way: they send SIGTERM, a polite "please stop" signal, to the main process, wait (10 seconds with docker stop, 30 by default in Kubernetes), and then send SIGKILL, which cannot be refused. Node running as the main process of a container has no default reaction to SIGTERM, so without a handler it ignores the signal, keeps running until the grace time ends, and is killed with exit code 137, which means killed by SIGKILL. Any request in progress is cut off.

The last line of our main.ts handles it: on SIGTERM, server.close() stops taking new connections, lets the open requests finish, and then the process exits with 0. Every deploy and every scale-down stops pods this way, so this one line decides whether users see cut-off requests.
read.see:
$ time docker stop svc
svc
docker stop svc  0.01s user 0.01s system 10% cpu 0.102 total
$ docker inspect svc --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'
0

lab.title: Build, lock down and stop a Node service in Docker
needs: Docker running (Docker Desktop, Colima or similar)
lab.goal: Build a two-stage image pinned by digest, run it as a non-root user on a read-only filesystem, prove both from inside, and stop it cleanly.

guess.q: A Dockerfile uses FROM node:24-bookworm-slim and has no USER line. You run docker exec <container> id. What does it print?

options.text: uid=1000(node), because the Node image runs as the node user
options.why: The official Node image creates a node user, but it does not switch to it. Without a USER line, everything runs as root.
Images run as root unless the Dockerfile says otherwise. That is why our Dockerfile ends with USER 10001:10001.

options.text: An error, because id is not installed in a slim image
options.why: Slim images still have the basic tools such as id, ls and sh. They just leave out compilers and documentation.

follow.say: Make a small service with one real dependency (zod) and a build script. This is what the image will run.
Pull the base image and keep its digest in a shell variable for the Dockerfile.
follow.do: docker pull node:24-bookworm-slim && DIGEST=$(docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' node:24-bookworm-slim | cut -d@ -f2) && echo $DIGEST
follow.see:
Digest: sha256:a5f4366e834695d5f363b920c104953a535d3a9864d1bdf74566a0ebe01daee5
Status: Image is up to date for node:24-bookworm-slim
docker.io/library/node:24-bookworm-slim
sha256:a5f4366e834695d5f363b920c104953a535d3a9864d1bdf74566a0ebe01daee5

follow.say: Write the two-stage Dockerfile. The EOF is not quoted this time, so the shell puts your digest into both FROM lines. Then build.
follow.do:
cat > Dockerfile <<EOF
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@${DIGEST} AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json .npmrc ./
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src src
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev --ignore-scripts

FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@${DIGEST}
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist dist
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]
EOF
printf 'node_modules\ndist\n' > .dockerignore && head -1 Dockerfile && docker build -t svc:dev .
follow.see:
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:a5f4366e834695d5f363b920c104953a535d3a9864d1bdf74566a0ebe01daee5 AS build
…
#15 unpacking to docker.io/library/svc:dev 0.1s done
#15 DONE 0.3s

follow.say: Run it with every lock on, read its log, and send it a comment.
follow.do: docker run -d --name svc -p 8080:8080 --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges svc:dev && sleep 2 && docker logs svc && curl -s -w '[%{http_code}]\n' -X POST localhost:8080/v1/comments -d '{"text":"from docker"}'

follow.say: Prove the locks from inside: who is the process, and can it write to its own folder or to /tmp?
follow.do: docker exec svc id; docker exec svc touch /app/x; docker exec svc touch /tmp/x
follow.see:
uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001
touch: cannot touch '/app/x': Read-only file system
touch: cannot touch '/tmp/x': Read-only file system

follow.say: Stop it the way a deploy would, and read the exit code.
follow.do: time docker stop svc; docker inspect svc --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'; docker rm svc
follow.see:
svc
docker stop svc  0.01s user 0.01s system 10% cpu 0.102 total
0
svc

lab.build: Find out for yourself what the SIGTERM line is worth. Delete the process.on("SIGTERM", …) line from src/main.ts, build the image as svc:nosig, run it (the locks do not matter for this test), and time docker stop again. Write down the seconds and the exit code and explain both in one sentence. Then put the line back, rebuild svc:dev, and clean up with docker rm and docker image rm svc:nosig.
checks: Both FROM lines in your Dockerfile end with @sha256: and the same digest.
docker logs svc printed listening on :8080, and the POST answered 1 comments [201].
docker exec svc id printed uid=10001, and both touch commands failed with Read-only file system.
docker stop with the SIGTERM handler took well under a second, and the exit code was 0.
Without the handler, docker stop took about 10 seconds and the exit code was 137.

solution.text:
sed -i.bak '/SIGTERM/d' src/main.ts
docker build -q -t svc:nosig .
docker run -d --name nosig svc:nosig
time docker stop nosig        # about 10 seconds
docker inspect nosig --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'   # 137
# Node ignored SIGTERM, so Docker waited its 10 seconds and then sent SIGKILL (128 + 9 = 137).
docker rm nosig && docker image rm svc:nosig
mv src/main.ts.bak src/main.ts && docker build -q -t svc:dev .

lab.fix: A new feature in the service writes a small cache file to /app/cache.json. It crashed in the container with EROFS: read-only file system, so a teammate removed --read-only from the run command and the securityContext, "just for this one service". Now the service can rewrite its own dist/ folder again. Repair it the other way round: run with --read-only plus --tmpfs /tmp, and explain why the cache belongs in /tmp, not in /app.
explain: What is in the build stage that is missing from the final image, and why does that matter for a service that holds a key?
Why does a tag such as node:24-bookworm-slim make builds change on their own, and how does a digest stop that?
What happens, second by second, when Docker stops a Node container that has no SIGTERM handler?
lab.done: The container answered 201 as uid 10001, could not write to /app or /tmp, and stopped in under a second with exit code 0; nothing named svc or nosig is left running.

check.q: Why does the Dockerfile copy package.json and the lockfile and run npm ci before it copies src/?

options.text: Because npm ci deletes the src folder if it already exists
options.why: npm ci only deletes node_modules. The order is about Docker's layer cache, not about npm.

options.text: So that editing source code does not throw away the cached install layer
options.why: Docker reuses a layer when its inputs are unchanged. The package files rarely change, so the slow install stays cached while src/ changes every day.

options.text: Because tsc must run before npm ci
options.why: It is the other way round: tsc comes from the dev dependencies, which npm ci installs.

check.q: A teammate says USER 10001 is enough and the three docker run flags are paranoid. What does --read-only add that a non-root user does not?

options.text: Nothing; a non-root user cannot write anywhere anyway
options.why: A non-root user can still write to /tmp and to any folder it owns. In the lab, the touch in /tmp failed only because of --read-only.

options.text: It makes the container start faster
options.why: Speed is not the point. The flag is about what a taken-over process can change.

options.text: No file can be written anywhere, so an attacker cannot drop a tool or a script into /tmp and run it later
options.why: Non-root stops the process from changing the app's files; read-only stops it from writing anything at all. Scratch space, if needed, is an in-memory --tmpfs.

check.q: During a deploy, a pod's container exits with code 137 after 30 seconds. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The process ignored SIGTERM, so it was killed with SIGKILL when the grace time ran out
options.why: 137 is 128 + 9, the number of SIGKILL. A Node process without a SIGTERM handler never stops by itself, so open requests are cut off.

options.text: The image's base was not pinned by digest
options.why: A moving base changes what you build, not how a running container stops.

options.text: The read-only filesystem stopped Node from writing its exit code
options.why: Exit codes are not written to the container's filesystem. The code comes from how the process ended.

p: Every platform service image (the gateway, broker, orchestrator, Slack app and checks) is built by one images workflow the way Byte's is: FROM node:24-bookworm-slim pinned by digest, npm ci --ignore-scripts, a tsc build, non-root user 10001, and CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] for the gateway. The images go to our container registry with immutable tags, so a tag can never be overwritten.

On the internal cluster the shared service chart runs each pod as user 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation and every capability dropped, so the locks hold even without docker run. The broker's container is hardened like Byte's broker container. The harness is the exception: it is not an image but one bundled file (lesson p1-7).

tickets.why: images.yml builds every service image: node:24-bookworm-slim by digest, npm ci --ignore-scripts, user 10001.
The gateway's image: pinned base, tsc build, non-root user, CMD node dist/server.js.
The gateway runs on the internal cluster as user 10001 with a read-only root filesystem.
The broker, orchestrator and Slack app pods run non-root and read-only, with all capabilities dropped.

words.plain: A Dockerfile with a build stage and a clean final stage that copies in only what runs.
A hash of an image's content (sha256:…). Unlike a tag, it always means the same bytes.
A user without root rights, set with USER 10001, that cannot change files owned by root.
A container started with --read-only cannot write any file. Scratch space comes from --tmpfs.
Small pieces of root power in Linux. --cap-drop ALL removes them all.
The polite stop signal Docker and Kubernetes send first. Without a handler, Node is killed later with exit code 137.

review.q: From memory: the five things that make our service image boring and hard to abuse.
review.a: A base pinned by digest, a multi-stage build that leaves tools and source behind, npm ci --ignore-scripts, USER 10001, and at run time read-only with every capability dropped and no-new-privileges. Plus a SIGTERM handler so it stops cleanly.

review.q: A teammate asks why the gateway image needs all this when the cluster is internal. What do you answer?
review.a: The gateway holds the Anthropic key and sees every model call. If one dependency is exploited, the locks decide what the attacker can do: as root with a writable disk and tools, almost anything; as uid 10001 on a read-only filesystem with no capabilities, almost nothing.

remember: Pin the base by digest, build in one stage and run in a clean one as user 10001, lock the filesystem and capabilities, prove it with docker exec, and handle SIGTERM.
